blocks.title: The Science of Measurement
blocks.subtitle: How sensors turn the physical world into numbers we can trust

blocks.text:
Science and engineering start with measurement. A thermometer, a pressure gauge or a radiosonde each performs the same task: it lets a physical quantity change something we can read, and then tells us how far to believe the reading.

This story follows a signal from the sensor to the screen and explains why calibration and uncertainty matter as much as the number itself.

blocks.heading: The measurement chain
blocks.text: Almost every modern instrument has the same stages. A **sensor** responds to the quantity. **Signal conditioning** amplifies and filters the weak response. A **converter** turns it into digital numbers, and **processing** applies the calibration and reports a value with its units.

steps.text: **Sense.** A sensing element changes with the measurand: a thermistor's resistance with temperature, a diaphragm's deflection with pressure, a capacitor's value with humidity.
**Condition.** Bridges, amplifiers and filters turn that small change into a clean voltage and reject noise outside the band of interest.
**Convert.** An analogue-to-digital converter samples the voltage. Its resolution and sampling rate set the finest detail that can be recorded.
**Calibrate.** The raw number is corrected using a relation established against a reference standard, then reported with its uncertainty.

points.text: Responds to temperature, pressure, humidity, strain, light or another quantity.

points.title: Signal conditioning
points.text: Excitation, amplification, filtering and linearisation of the raw sensor output.

points.title: A/D converter
points.text: Samples and quantises the signal; more bits give finer resolution.

points.title: Processing
points.text: Applies calibration coefficients, compensates for temperature and checks data quality.

points.title: Display and telemetry
points.text: Shows, stores or transmits the result, as a radiosonde does by radio during its ascent.

blocks.heading: Accuracy is not precision
blocks.text: **Precision** describes how closely repeated readings agree with each other. **Accuracy** describes how close they are to the true value. An instrument can be precise and wrong. **Calibration** against a traceable reference removes known errors, and an **uncertainty** statement says honestly how much doubt remains.

items.title: Accuracy
items.text: Closeness of a measurement to the true value of the quantity.

items.title: Resolution
items.text: The smallest change an instrument can detect or display.

items.title: Traceability
items.text: An unbroken chain of calibrations linking a reading back to national and international standards.

items.title: Uncertainty
items.text: A quantified range within which the true value is believed to lie, with a stated confidence.

items.title: Drift
items.text: Slow change of an instrument's response over time; the reason calibration is repeated.

items.title: Response time
items.text: How quickly a sensor follows a change. A slow sensor smears rapid variations.

blocks.heading: Hard problems in measurement
blocks.text: Field instruments face heat, cold, moisture, vibration and radiation that laboratory instruments never see. Designers must limit drift, compensate for cross-sensitivity, protect sensors from solar heating and icing, and keep power and weight low. Comparing instruments from different makers fairly is a discipline in itself.

blocks.question: A scale always reads 0.5 kg too high, but repeats to within 1 g. It is:
blocks.explanation: Readings agree closely (precise) but carry a constant offset from the true value (inaccurate). Calibration can remove the offset.

blocks.question: What does 'traceability' mean in measurement?
options: The data are stored in a database
The reading is linked to recognised standards through an unbroken chain of calibrations
The sensor has a serial number
The signal is transmitted by radio
blocks.explanation: Traceability lets results from different instruments and laboratories be compared on a common basis.

blocks.heading: Key terms and next steps
blocks.text:
**Measurand**: the quantity being measured. **Transducer**: a device that converts one form of energy or signal into another. **Hysteresis**: a reading that depends on whether the quantity is rising or falling. **Radiosonde**: a balloon-borne instrument measuring pressure, temperature, humidity and wind.
